title: Scientists Burned Scrolls on Purpose — And It Might Unlock a Buried Library
summary:
Imagine a library from 2,000 years ago. Then imagine a volcano burying it in ash. That's what happened in Herculaneum, an ancient Roman city in Italy, when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 C.E. More than a thousand papyrus scrolls turned into black, crispy lumps. You can't unroll them — they'd crumble into dust.

So Douglas Seiler tried something wild. He bought papyrus and ink, then paid high school students to write on it using Star Wars lines and Bible passages. Then he burned it all. Why? To test an idea about ink.

Here's the trick: if ancient ink had lead in it, lead blocks X-rays way better than burnt paper — about 25 times better. So a computer can scan the scroll and show the hidden letters without opening it. Seiler's test worked!

Now researchers want to scan the real scrolls. About 1,800 survive in Italy, France, and England. Some might hold books nobody has read since Roman times. "The stakes are the largest in the history of Greek literature," said Leah Packard-Grams, who helped with the project. That's a pretty big deal.
why_it_matters: It shows that a strange, messy experiment — even one that means burning your own writing on purpose — can be the key to opening a library of books nobody has read for 2,000 years.

background_read: Mount Vesuvius (a volcano in Italy) also buried the nearby city of Pompeii in 79 C.E. Ash covered whole streets and buildings there, which is why archaeologists can still study them today.
Papyrus was made from a tall plant that grew along the River Nile, and sheets were rolled up instead of folded into pages — that is why we call them scrolls.
X-rays are the same invisible light doctors use to see the bones inside your body, and heavy metals like lead stop them — that is why you wear a heavy apron at the dentist.
Article_Structure: WHO: Douglas Seiler, who burned his own papyrus-and-ink test scrolls, high school students who did the writing, and Leah Packard-Grams, who helped with the project.
WHAT: The test worked — lead in ancient ink lets a computer scan show hidden letters without ever unrolling a scroll.
WHERE: The scrolls are from Herculaneum in Italy, and about 1,800 of them survive in Italy, France, and England.
WHY: If the trick works on the real scrolls, researchers could read books nobody has opened since Roman times.

perspectives.description: They think the lead-ink trick could unlock Greek literature that has been locked inside black lumps for centuries, which is why they call the stakes the biggest in the history of Greek literature.
They worry that the real scrolls are extremely fragile, and that scanning or moving them could destroy the only copies we have.
They point out that not every ancient ink may have contained lead, so the method might work on only some of the surviving scrolls.
